name: Carrowfield Waxed Canvas Barn Jacket
description:
A heavy waxed canvas barn jacket in faded tobacco brown, cut wide through the shoulders with a corduroy collar and four brass-snap patch pockets. The wax finish has been applied thick enough to bead water without any tech assistance — just old-fashioned textile chemistry. The lining is a coarse plaid flannel, warm but not suffocating, and the whole thing smells faintly of linseed oil and machine grease after a week of wear.

Carrowfield is a mid-tier independent label out of the old Milwaukee corridor, making workwear-adjacent pieces for people who actually work. This jacket is popular with Tier 2 tradespeople, delivery runners, and outer-district shop owners who need something that holds up to weather, tool catches, and the general abuse of a working day. It softens and darkens with age in a way that makes each jacket look unique after six months of use.
what_it_says: You work with your hands and you buy things that last. You're not performing toughness — you've earned it.
story_hooks: A character finds a crumpled note in the breast pocket of a secondhand Carrowfield — an address, a date three weeks past, and a name they recognize from a missing persons report.
The jacket's wax finish, it turns out, is chemically similar enough to a specific industrial solvent that it lets the wearer pass a contamination checkpoint unquestioned.
A Carrowfield factory worker is selling a batch of jackets with a subtle alteration sewn into the lining — something a union organizer asked them to hide.

physical_description.visual_profile: A substantial, broad-shouldered work jacket with a distinctly vintage silhouette. The faded tobacco brown waxed canvas reads as weathered and lived-in, suggesting hard use and genuine durability. Sits between utilitarian and refined—workwear with character. The wide cut and generous proportions convey utility without appearing oversized or fashion-forward.
physical_description.fit: Wide through the shoulders and chest with a relaxed, room-to-move cut. Not tailored, but not baggy—designed to accommodate layers and tool belts. Sleeves are straight and full-length. The hem hits at the hip, allowing easy movement for climbing, reaching, and bending.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavy waxed canvas—tightly woven cotton treated with thick linseed oil-based wax coating. The finish is tactile and water-beading, with a subtle sheen that deepens with patina.
physical_description.texture: Slightly stiff when new, developing a softer, more supple hand with wear. The surface has a subtle crackle pattern from wax aging. Corduroy collar provides contrast—soft, napped texture that ages to a duller pile.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: faded tobacco brown with warm, earthy undertones. The wax gives it an amber luminosity in certain light. No intentional pattern, but natural color variation and darkening appear with wear. Brass hardware adds warm metallic accents.
physical_description.closures: Four brass-snap patch pockets (functional, not decorative). No center closure visible in description—likely buttons or snaps down the front (unstated but implied for barn jacket construction).
distinctive_features: Corduroy collar in matching tobacco tone
Four large brass-snap patch pockets with visible topstitching
Thick wax finish that beads water without electronic assistance
Coarse plaid flannel lining (visible at collar and cuffs)
Linseed oil and machine grease patina develops naturally with use
Darkens and softens with age—each jacket becomes unique
No visible tech integration or augmentation compatibility
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2–3 boundary. Affordable enough for working-class tradespeople and delivery runners, quality high enough to justify mid-range pricing. Signals someone who works with their hands, values durability over status.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by outer-district shop owners, HVAC runners, delivery couriers, and independent technicians who actually use their tools. Suggests Midwestern practical sensibility, rejection of disposable fashion, and honest labor. Not corpo (too rough), not sub-grade (too well-made). Blue-collar heritage, dignified wear.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and patched. Oil stains from regular use, possible small tears or snags repaired with matching canvas. Color darkened unevenly from sweat, rain, and sun exposure. Wax develops a lived-in crackle. Linseed oil smell fades but never fully disappears. Brass develops patina. Each jacket tells a story of its wearer's trade.

image_prompt: A weathered waxed canvas barn jacket displayed on a broad-shouldered mannequin or worn by a middle-aged worker model with calloused hands, set in a moody industrial workspace—maybe a tool-cluttered garage or warehouse corner with soft amber overhead lighting. The tobacco brown canvas catches warm light, emphasizing the subtle sheen and aging crackle. Close-up details of the brass snaps, corduroy collar, and flannel lining visible. Faint oil stains and patina on the fabric. Dark, gritty urban backdrop. --ar 2:3 --v 6
